rows.question: I rent in San Francisco. When can my landlord end my tenancy? Answer as of 2026-10-01.
rows.answer:
As of 2026-10-01, two just-cause rules were in force in San Francisco. One is city law and one is state law. This is a city-level answer, not one for your specific building.

**City rule: San Francisco Rent Ordinance § 37.9(a)** (in force)
> "In order to evict a tenant from a rental unit covered by the Rent Ordinance, a landlord must have a "just cause" reason that is the dominant motive for pursuing the eviction."

The listed reasons include:
- nonpayment or habitual late payment
- substantial breach
- nuisance
- illegal use
- refusal of lawful access
- specified owner or family occupancy
- sale after an approved condominium conversion
- demolition or rehabilitation
- Ellis Act withdrawal
- lead remediation

HomeRule's summary of the list is cut off, and it says the list includes "specified …" further reasons. Its source is https://sf.gov/information/overview-just-cause-evictions.

**State rule: Cal. Civil Code § 1946.2** (in force since Apr 1, 2024, through 2030-01-01)
> "after a tenant has continuously and lawfully occupied a residential real property for 12 months, the owner of the residential real property shall not terminate a tenancy without just cause"

- **Occupancy time:** the 12 months of continuous, lawful occupancy is the usual threshold. If additional adult tenants were added before an existing tenant reached 24 months, then either all tenants must have occupied for 12 months or more, or at least one must have occupied for 24 months or more.
- **Relationship to the city rule:** HomeRule says the state rule "steps back where a stricter local rule covers the building."

**Facts I don't have**
HomeRule doesn't know which rule governs your building without these:
- whether the owner lives in the building
- whether the building is subsidized
- the number of units
- the type of building
- the year built (relevant to rent control)
- how long you've lived there

HomeRule also notes that some tenancies exempt from rent-increase limits are still subject to eviction protections.

Full rule pages are linked from https://yourhomerule.com/j/CA-SAN-FRANCISCO.

**To confirm for your situation:** call the San Francisco Rent Board at 415-252-4600 (https://sf.gov/speak-rent-board-counselor). HomeRule has not yet checked this number, so confirm it before you call.

rows.question: I'm moving from Boston to San Francisco. How is my rent situation changing?
rows.answer:
Here is how the rules compare as of 2026-10-04. Which rule applies to a given building depends on the building's facts.

## Rent increases
- **Boston:**
  - Mass. Gen. Laws ch. 40P, § 4 is in force: "No city or town may enact, maintain or enforce rent control of any kind, except that any city or town that accepts this chapter may adopt rent control regulation that provides:"
  - Mass. H.3744 would let Boston adopt rent stabilization. It is proposed, not law.
- **San Francisco:**
  - San Francisco Rent Ordinance § 37.3, in force: "For rent-controlled units, the annual allowable increase amount effective March 1, 2026 through February 28, 2027 is 1.6%." Newly built units that first got a Certificate of Occupancy after June 13, 1979 are exempt.
  - Cal. Civ. Code § 1947.12, in force since Apr 1, 2024: an owner "shall not, over the course of any 12-month period, increase the gross rental rate for a dwelling or a unit more than 5 percent plus the percentage change in the cost of living, or 10 percent, whichever is lower". It has statutory exceptions.

## Eviction protection
- **Boston:**
  - Mass. Gen. Laws ch. 186, § 11: "fourteen days' notice to quit, given in writing by the landlord to the tenant, shall be sufficient to determine the lease". HomeRule lists this as the 14-day notice for nonpayment.
  - Boston City Ordinances § 10-11.7, in force since Nov 6, 2020: "The Notice of Tenants' Rights and Resources must be delivered at the same time as the Notice to Quit."
- **San Francisco:**
  - San Francisco Rent Ordinance § 37.9(a): a landlord "must have a 'just cause' reason that is the dominant motive for pursuing the eviction."
  - Cal. Civil Code § 1946.2, in force since Apr 1, 2024: "after a tenant has continuously and lawfully occupied a residential real property for 12 months, the owner of the residential real property shall not terminate a tenancy without just cause". It has exclusions.

## Deposits
- **Boston:** Mass. Gen. Laws ch. 186, § 15B limits amounts at the start of a tenancy. HomeRule's key value is that the security deposit may not exceed the first month's rent.
- **San Francisco:**
  - Cal. Civ. Code § 1950.5(c)(1), in force since Jul 1, 2024: a landlord "shall not demand or receive security, however denominated, in an amount or value in excess of an amount equal to one month's rent".
  - San Francisco Rent Ordinance § 37.6 sets deposit interest at 4.2% for March 1, 2026 – February 28, 2027.

## Application fees
- **Boston:**
  - Mass. Gen. Laws ch. 112, § 87DDD½, in force since Aug 1, 2025: "Any fee shall only be paid by the party, lessor or tenant who originally engaged and entered into a contract with the licensed broker or salesperson."
  - Mass. Gen. Laws ch. 186, § 15B(1)(b) limits what can be required at the start of a tenancy. HomeRule gives no separate key value for it.
- **San Francisco:** Cal. Civ. Code § 1950.6. The key value is $30 per applicant, adjusted annually for CPI beginning January 1, 1998. The fee is limited to the "actual out-of-pocket costs of gathering information concerning the applicant".

## Screening
- **Boston:**
  - Mass. Gen. Laws ch. 151B, § 4(6)(a) bars refusing to rent because of protected characteristics. It covers housing described as publicly assisted, multiple dwelling, or contiguously located.
  - Boston Fair Housing Regulations apply to housing in Boston.
  - The Boston Fair Chance Tenant Selection Policy bars blanket criminal-record denials. It applies only to providers with DND funding or land, or with income-restricted units under the BPDA Inclusionary Development Policy.
- **San Francisco:** Cal. Gov. Code § 12955: "This law prohibits people or entities that provide housing from discriminating against or harassing tenants, homeowners, residents, their guests, housing or mortgage applicants, home buyers, and others."

## Rent-setting software
- **Boston:** Mass. S.2983 and H.5222 would restrict algorithmic rent setting. Both are proposed, not law.
- **San Francisco:**
  - San Francisco Rent Ordinance § 37.10C, in force since Oct 14, 2024: "The law prohibits the sale or use of algorithmic devices to set rents or manage occupancy levels for residential units in San Francisco."
  - Cal. Bus. & Prof. Code § 16729(a), in force since Jan 1, 2026, concerns common pricing algorithms used to restrain trade.

## Unknowns
- I don't know your SF building's age, type, or whether it is rent-controlled. Those facts decide whether the 1.6% city limit, the state cap, or an exemption applies.
- HomeRule lists "conditions not extracted yet" for several of these rules.

Full pages: [Boston](https://yourhomerule.com/j/MA-BOSTON) and [San Francisco](https://yourhomerule.com/j/CA-SAN-FRANCISCO). The tool result didn't include contacts. Before you rely on any of this, confirm it with the San Francisco Rent Board or a local tenant counselor.

Not legal advice.
